subject: Critical Thinking
title: Moral Intuition: That Gut Feeling of Right and Wrong
description: One-minute skill: Moral Intuition: That Gut Feeling of Right and Wrong.

hook.text: You see someone kick a dog.

buildup.text: Moral intuitions: automatic, emotional responses to ethical situations that occur before conscious reasoning.

discovery.text: Jonathan Haidt's 'social intuitionist model': moral judgments are usually intuitions first, reasoning second.

twist.text: Haidt's dumbfounding experiments: people say incest is wrong but can't explain why. The intuition has no argument.

climax.text: Intuitions are fast & often right – but they can be biased, culturally conditioned, & manipulated.

punchline.text: Your moral gut is usually right.

quiz.question: What did Haidt's research show about moral judgments?
options: They typically begin as emotional intuitions, with reasoning following after

details.summary: Moral intuitions are immediate, instinctive judgments about right and wrong that arise before conscious reasoning. They serve as data points for ethical theories but can be unreliable due to biases and cultural conditioning.
details.whyItMatters: Every moral theory must either explain or override intuitions, making them the starting point of all ethical reasoning.
takeaways: Moral intuitions are fast, pre-reflective moral judgments
They can conflict with rational analysis
Both trusting and ignoring them entirely is problematic

faq.question: Should we trust our moral intuitions when making ethical decisions?
faq.answer: Intuitions are useful starting points but unreliable as final verdicts. They can be shaped by bias, culture, and emotion, so reflective scrutiny is essential.

faq.question: What role do moral intuitions play in philosophical arguments?
faq.answer: Philosophers use widely shared intuitions as evidence for or against ethical theories. A theory that wildly contradicts common moral sense needs very strong justification.
